You are a debugging assistant. You have access to the source code of the system under test (SUT), the failing test case (signature + snippet), the current issue report describing the failure.

Your task is to provide a step-by-step explanation of how the bug occurred using all available evidence:
– the failing test (signature + snippet),
– the current bug report,
– and code snippets of methods from the SUT.

Some identifiers in the current bug report may be anonymized with placeholders (e.g., C#.M#). If the same token (e.g., C1) appears multiple times, it consistently refers to the same class (C) or method (M) throughout the report. These tokens are not complete qualified names. Always confirm actual identifiers by inspecting the source code using get_code_snippet.

You will be given 9 opportunities to interact with functions to gather information for the debugging. An example diagnosis would look like follows.

Title: Diagnosis
Details: The corresponding issue report describes that tooltip text in the UI is displayed with HTML entities such as " instead of the intended characters. This strongly suggests a missing escaping or decoding step in tooltip generation. Inspecting the implementation of StandardToolTipTagFragmentGenerator.generateToolTipFragment reveals that it directly returns the toolTipText without applying any escaping. Recent issue reports mention similar encoding or escaping problems in related UI components, reinforcing the suspicion that this method lacks proper handling. The behavior observed in the code matches the issue report's symptoms, indicating that missing escaping in this method is the likely root cause.

After providing this diagnosis, you will be prompted to suggest which methods would be the best locations to be fixed. The answers should be in the form of `ClassName.MethodName(ArgType1, ArgType2, ...)` without commentary (one per line), as your answer will be automatically processed before finally being presented to the user.

messages.content:
Title: Diagnosis

Details:
The bug report describes that the `MultiDirectional.iterateSimplex` method loops forever if the starting point is already the correct solution. Looking at the implementation of `iterateSimplex`, we see it contains an infinite loop (`while (true)`) that is supposed to exit by returning when certain conditions are met after performing reflection, expansion, or contraction steps on the simplex.

The current code logic in `iterateSimplex` is:
- Save the original simplex vertices and identify the best vertex.
- Perform a reflection step to get a reflected simplex.
- If the reflected simplex is better (according to the comparator) than the best, then optionally perform an expansion. Depending on comparisons, accept the expanded or reflected simplex and return (exit).
- Otherwise, perform a contraction step and, if better than the best, accept the contracted simplex and return (exit).
- If neither reflection nor contraction improved on the best value, the loop continues without a termination condition.

The potential problem is that in cases where the starting point is the correct solution (the best), the reflection and contraction steps may not produce any improvement. This leads to none of the return conditions triggered, thus the `while (true)` loops infinitely without termination.

Additionally, the code snippet reveals that in the case of contraction success (line 90 `if (comparator.compare(contracted, best) < 0)`), there is a comment "// accept the contracted simplex" but the actual acceptance (updating `simplex = ...`) is not visible. This may be a formatting issue or missing code, but that part is critical to confirm.

The `evaluateNewSimplex` method generates a new simplex by reflecting or transforming around the best vertex, then evaluates the function values and sorts the simplex with the comparator.

Given this flow, if the starting solution is already optimal (best vertex cannot be improved by reflection or contraction), the algorithm never hits the return statements that break the infinite loop, so it loops forever.

This diagnosis aligns with the observed failure that the optimizer hangs when started at the correct solution.

Hence, the cause of the infinite loop is missing or insufficient checks for termination or convergence when no improvement can be made, causing the infinite loop in `MultiDirectional.iterateSimplex`.

The test `testMinimizeMaximize` starts from a point near to a known minimum or maximum, which likely triggers this infinite loop.

# Next step recommendation
- Inspect if there are missing updates to the simplex on contraction acceptance.
- Confirm if convergence checks or termination conditions are missing when no improvement is achieved.
- Suggest adding proper termination conditions in `iterateSimplex` to handle "no improvement" cases.

This is how the bug occurred in detail based on the provided test and code.

Your answer will be processed automatically, so make sure to only answer with the accurate signatures of all likely culprits (in `ClassName.MethodName(ArgType1, ArgType2, ...)` format), without commentary (one per line).
